headline: The biggest adjustment is swapping the Philippines' warm, touch-friendly, tip-and-chat style for Japan's quieter, bow-first, no-tipping, order-for-yourself rhythm.

watch_outs.title: No tipping at restaurants
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you check for a service charge and otherwise leave about 10% in cash with the server.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan tipping is not customary and is politely declined; service is included in the bill.
watch_outs.do: Skip the tip and thank your server with a genuine 'gochisōsama deshita' as you leave.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not leave cash on the table or press money into a server's hand.

watch_outs.title: Bow, don't cheek-kiss
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines a light cheek-to-cheek greeting with a soft 'mwah' is common among friends and family.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan a bow, or a soft handshake if offered first, is the standard greeting; cheek kisses are not.
watch_outs.do: Bow slightly when meeting colleagues and family, deepening the bow for senior people.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not lean in for a cheek kiss unless your host clearly initiates it.

watch_outs.title: Order your own dish
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines sharing dishes family-style and ordering a few plates for the table is the norm.
watch_outs.to_norm: In many Japanese restaurants, especially small ramen, yakitori and set-meal shops, each person orders at least one item.
watch_outs.do: Have every person at the table order their own dish or set.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not order one dish to share in a small restaurant with limited seating.

watch_outs.title: Chopstick funeral taboos
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you eat with fork and spoon, so chopstick rules rarely come up.
watch_outs.to_norm: Standing chopsticks upright in rice or passing food chopstick-to-chopstick echoes funeral rituals in Japan.
watch_outs.do: Rest chopsticks on the holder or across your bowl when not eating.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not stick chopsticks upright in rice or pass food directly between chopsticks.

watch_outs.title: Gift with both hands
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines a modest wrapped gift is welcome and it is fine if it isn't opened right away.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan a modest, nicely wrapped gift such as regional omiyage is expected, presented with both hands and often set aside unopened.
watch_outs.do: Bring a small wrapped specialty from home and offer it with both hands.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not expect your gift to be opened in front of you or push them to open it.

watch_outs.title: Decline food gently
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you hesitate, then accept at least a small portion or ask to take some home rather than refuse outright.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan you decline softly with a phrase like 'mō kekkō desu' or mention you're full, and close with 'gochisōsama deshita'.
watch_outs.do: Accept a little if you can, and thank your host warmly at the end of the meal.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not refuse bluntly or leave without thanking your host for the food.

watch_outs.title: Feet tucked on tatami
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines foot position is a minor issue, mainly avoiding feet on furniture at a home visit.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan, when seated on tatami, tuck your feet under you or sit cross-legged neatly rather than stretching legs toward others or the alcove.
watch_outs.do: Sit neatly with feet tucked under you on tatami.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not stretch your legs out toward other people or the tokonoma alcove.

watch_outs.title: Punctuality in business
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines relaxed 'Filipino time' is fine socially, though business meetings expect you on time.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan arriving a few minutes early for meetings and appointments is the standard.
watch_outs.do: Plan to arrive five minutes early for every business meeting.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not treat a business meeting with the relaxed timing you might use for a social gathering.

watch_outs.title: Slurping is a compliment
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you eat noodle soup quietly with a spoon, and loud slurping isn't a compliment.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan audible slurping in a casual noodle shop is a compliment to the chef.
watch_outs.do: Slurp naturally if it feels comfortable in a casual noodle shop.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not force loud slurping if it feels unnatural, and keep it quiet in formal settings.

watch_outs.title: Head-pats only for kids
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines head-patting is fine with children you know but risky with adults, especially elders.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Japan head-pats are fine for children you know well but too familiar with adults.
watch_outs.do: Use a nod, bow or verbal compliment with adults instead.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not pat an adult colleague or elder on the head.
